points.title: L'inversion stylistique après certains adverbes
points.explanationEn:
One of the clearest fingerprints of soutenu written French — the kind you meet constantly in legal and economic writing — is a subject-verb inversion triggered simply by placing certain adverbs at the very front of a clause. This has no equivalent reflex in modern English, where only a handful of frozen literary phrases ('rarely have I seen...', 'never had she imagined...') behave this way. In French it's a live, productive rule: when peut-être ('perhaps'), aussi (here meaning 'therefore/consequently', not 'also'), ainsi ('thus'), sans doute ('probably'), à peine ('scarcely/hardly'), or du moins ('at least') opens a clause, the subject and verb typically invert.

With a pronoun subject, the inversion is direct: 'Peut-être devrions-nous réviser cette clause' (Perhaps we should revise this clause). With a noun subject, French cannot invert the noun itself — instead it keeps the noun in place and adds an echoing pronoun after the verb, the same reprise pronominale mechanism used in formal questions: 'Ainsi, le tribunal a-t-il tranché en faveur du plaignant' (Thus the court ruled in favor of the plaintiff) — not 'ainsi a tranché le tribunal.' Skipping this inversion and just bolting the adverb onto normal word order ('Peut-être nous devrions réviser cette clause') is grammatically wrong, not merely less elegant — it's one of the few inversions in French that isn't optional stylistic flourish but an actual rule triggered by the adverb's sentence-initial position.

The single biggest trap here is aussi, a genuine false friend at the start of a sentence. Mid-sentence or as a simple additive ('je suis aussi fatigué' — I'm also tired), aussi means 'also' and triggers nothing. But at the very start of a clause, aussi shifts to mean 'therefore, consequently' — a logical connector, not an additive one — and it demands inversion exactly like the others: 'Le contrat était ambigu ; aussi le juge a-t-il demandé des clarifications' (The contract was ambiguous; the judge therefore asked for clarifications). Misreading this aussi as 'also' produces a nonsensical translation and also causes learners to skip the required inversion.

There's a useful escape hatch worth knowing for peut-être specifically: you can avoid the inversion altogether by inserting que after it and keeping normal word order — 'Peut-être que nous devrions réviser cette clause' means exactly the same thing and is entirely acceptable, including in writing. This is a good option under time pressure, but relying on it exclusively means never practicing the inversion itself, which is precisely the marker that signals genuine command of soutenu register in legal and economic writing.

examples.fr: Peut-être devrions-nous renégocier les termes du contrat.
examples.en: Perhaps we should renegotiate the terms of the contract.

examples.fr: Peut-être que le tribunal rendra sa décision avant la fin du mois.
examples.en: Perhaps the court will hand down its decision before the end of the month.
examples.note: 'Peut-être que' + normal word order: the accepted alternative to inversion.

examples.fr: Le marché s'est effondré ; aussi les investisseurs ont-ils retiré leurs fonds.
examples.en: The market collapsed; the investors therefore withdrew their funds.

examples.fr: Ainsi s'achève l'audience de ce matin.
examples.note: 'Ainsi' + inversion with a pronoun subject understood in the verb form.

examples.fr: Ainsi, le gouvernement a-t-il décidé de revoir la fiscalité des entreprises.
examples.en: Thus, the government decided to review corporate taxation.
examples.note: Reprise pronominale: 'a-t-il' echoes the noun subject 'le gouvernement'.

examples.fr: Sans doute faudra-t-il modifier la clause de résiliation.
examples.en: The termination clause will probably need to be amended.

examples.fr: À peine le contrat avait-il été signé que des désaccords sont apparus.
examples.en: No sooner had the contract been signed than disagreements arose.
examples.note: 'À peine' + inversion, classic 'no sooner... than' pattern.

examples.fr: Du moins peut-on affirmer que la loi manque de clarté.
examples.en: At the very least, one can say that the law lacks clarity.

examples.fr: L'entreprise a licencié massivement ; aussi le syndicat a-t-il appelé à la grève.
examples.en: The company laid off massively; the union therefore called for a strike.

commonMistakes: Reading sentence-initial 'aussi' as 'also' instead of 'therefore', which both misreads the logic of the sentence and causes the required inversion to be skipped.

Placing the adverb at the start of the clause but leaving normal subject-verb order intact, e.g. 'Peut-être nous devrions...' instead of 'Peut-être devrions-nous...' or 'Peut-être que nous devrions...'.
Inverting a noun subject directly instead of using the reprise pronominale, e.g. 'Ainsi a tranché le tribunal' instead of 'Ainsi le tribunal a-t-il tranché'.
Applying this inversion after adverbs that don't trigger it (like heureusement or malheureusement), over-generalizing the rule to every sentence-initial adverb.
Using this inversion in casual spoken French, where it reads as noticeably stiff and overly formal rather than natural.
whyItTrips: Modern English only inverts after a fronted adverb in a small set of frozen literary expressions, so English speakers have no live productive habit of triggering inversion this way — it feels like an exception rather than a rule.

Aussi doing double duty as both 'also' (mid-sentence, no inversion) and 'therefore' (sentence-initial, inversion required) is a genuine false-friend trap with no parallel in English, where 'also' and 'therefore' are never the same word.
The reprise pronominale needed for noun subjects adds an extra layer most learners haven't automated even for formal questions, let alone for this less-frequently-taught adverb-triggered inversion.

points.title: Dont et les pronoms relatifs complexes
points.explanationEn:
Formal legal and economic writing leans heavily on complex sentences built from relative clauses, and getting the relative pronoun right — dont, lequel/laquelle, auquel, duquel, and their plural forms — is one of the clearest markers of command over written register at B2 and beyond. The core principle: French chooses its relative pronoun based on which preposition the verb or noun inside the relative clause requires, not on the antecedent's role in English (where 'whose', 'which', and 'that' get stretched to cover almost everything).

Dont is the pronoun for any relative clause where the missing element is introduced by de: it replaces de qui, duquel, or de laquelle whenever a simple de-relationship is involved, and it covers three distinct English translations depending on context — 'whose' for possession ('l'entreprise dont le PDG a démissionné', the company whose CEO resigned), 'of which/about which' for verbs and expressions built with de ('le dossier dont nous avons discuté', the file we discussed — from discuter de), and simply 'that... of' for nouns paired with de ('un projet dont l'ampleur surprend', a project whose scale is surprising — from l'ampleur de). Because dont already contains de, you must never add a second de anywhere else in the clause — 'le livre dont j'ai besoin de' is a doubling error; dont alone does the whole job of avoir besoin de.

When there's no explicit antecedent noun to attach dont to, French uses ce dont: 'Voici ce dont nous avons besoin pour conclure l'accord' (Here is what we need to close the deal). This parallels ce que/ce qui from indirect questions, but specifically for the de-relationship.

For every preposition other than de, French uses the lequel family instead, which agrees in gender and number with its antecedent and contracts with à and de exactly like the definite article does: à + lequel → auquel, à + lesquels → auxquels, à + lesquelles → auxquelles. 'Le tribunal auquel l'affaire a été renvoyée' (the court to which the case was referred) uses auquel because renvoyer is followed by à. With compound prepositions that happen to end in de (à côté de, au sujet de, en raison de, à l'égard de), dont is not used — instead you need duquel/de laquelle/desquels, because dont can only replace a bare, simple de, not de as the tail end of a longer preposition: 'l'immeuble au sujet duquel le litige a éclaté' (the building the dispute arose about), never 'l'immeuble dont le litige a éclaté au sujet.' Choosing correctly between dont and duquel/de laquelle in these compound-preposition cases is exactly the kind of fine distinction that marks genuinely advanced written French.

examples.fr: L'entreprise dont le chiffre d'affaires a doublé cherche de nouveaux investisseurs.
examples.en: The company whose revenue has doubled is seeking new investors.
examples.note: Dont expressing possession (le chiffre d'affaires de l'entreprise).

examples.fr: Voici les documents dont vous aurez besoin pour signer le contrat.
examples.en: Here are the documents you will need to sign the contract.
examples.note: Dont from 'avoir besoin de' — no extra 'de' allowed elsewhere in the clause.

examples.fr: C'est une clause dont la portée juridique reste incertaine.
examples.en: It's a clause whose legal scope remains uncertain.

examples.fr: Voici ce dont il s'agit dans cette affaire.
examples.en: Here is what this case is about.
examples.note: Ce dont: no explicit antecedent, from 's'agir de'.

examples.fr: Le tribunal auquel l'affaire a été renvoyée rendra sa décision en mars.
examples.en: The court to which the case was referred will rule in March.

examples.fr: La société avec laquelle nous négocions est cotée en bourse.
examples.en: The company with which we are negotiating is publicly traded.
examples.note: 'Avec' + laquelle: not 'de', so dont is impossible here.

examples.fr: Les obligations auxquelles l'entreprise doit se conformer figurent dans l'annexe.
examples.en: The obligations the company must comply with are listed in the appendix.

examples.fr: L'immeuble au sujet duquel le litige a éclaté appartient à la municipalité.
examples.en: The building the dispute arose about belongs to the municipality.
examples.note: Compound preposition ending in 'de': duquel required, not dont.

examples.fr: C'est précisément ce à quoi les actionnaires s'opposent.
examples.en: That is precisely what the shareholders are opposed to.
examples.note: Ce à quoi: no antecedent, from 's'opposer à'.

commonMistakes: Adding a redundant second 'de' after dont, e.g. 'le contrat dont nous avons besoin de' instead of the correct 'le contrat dont nous avons besoin'.
Using dont with a compound preposition ending in de (au sujet de, à côté de, en raison de) instead of switching to duquel/de laquelle/desquels.
Using 'que' where dont is required, e.g. 'le projet que l'ampleur surprend' instead of 'le projet dont l'ampleur surprend'.

Forgetting the à + lequel contraction and writing 'à lequel' or 'à laquelle' incorrectly instead of the contracted 'auquel'/'à laquelle' (laquelle does not contract, but auquel/auxquels/auxquelles do).
Keeping the noun in its original position after dont instead of moving it immediately after dont, e.g. writing 'dont a démissionné le PDG' instead of 'dont le PDG a démissionné'.
whyItTrips: English 'whose' and 'of which' flatten every de-relationship into one all-purpose word regardless of whether it marks possession, a verb's required preposition, or a noun complement, so English speakers have no instinct to check which underlying preposition (de vs à vs a compound) governs the clause.
Because dont already absorbs the 'de', mentally translating word-for-word from an English 'of which I need' produces a doubled 'de' that isn't there in the English original at all.
The lequel/laquelle/auquel/duquel family inflects for gender and number and contracts with à and de, a level of morphological agreement relative pronouns simply don't carry in English.
